originalGroup.material:
The notebook beside the robot

At our robotics club exhibition, visitors admired the machine that followed a black line across the floor. My friend wrote its code; another designed its body. I stood behind them, unsure what to say about my own ____1____.

For weeks, I had checked batteries, labelled wires and written down what happened during tests. It seemed less ____2____ than making the robot move. When a visitor asked who had built it, I almost said, "They did."

Then the robot stopped halfway along the line. My friend opened the computer, ready to change the ____3____. I remembered an entry in my notebook: the same sudden stop had happened when one battery connection was loose.

"Can we check this first?" I asked. A wire had slipped. Once it was secured, the robot ____4____ its journey.

The visitor turned to me. "How did you know?"

I showed her the notebook. Each test had a date, a description and a drawing of the connections. The pages were not tidy, but they helped us ____5____ today's problem with an earlier one.

Our teacher asked me to put the notebook beside the display. I ____6____, worried that its crossed-out lines would look careless. She said those changes showed what the team had actually tried.

As the afternoon continued, several visitors stopped to read it. One asked why we had ____7____ a larger wheel. I could answer because I had recorded the reason, not just the final choice.

I began to describe my role more ____8____. I had not written the main code, but I had helped keep our learning from ____9____ between tests. The robot's smooth movement depended on more than the parts visitors could ____10____.

My friend requested a copy for our next design. I felt ____11____, but the notes mattered because they helped ____12____. A team needed different kinds of ____13____. I had already been doing a ____14____ job. At the next meeting, I opened a fresh notebook and asked what we needed to ____15____.

During an exchange visit, I entered a small café alone. The menu was completely ____1____ to me. I tried asking the waiter what she would ____2____, but she shook her head. She could not ____3____ my English question.

For a moment, I felt ____4____. I wanted to leave before making a bigger mistake. The waiter, however, remained ____5____. She brought a pencil and a piece of paper.

I drew a bowl with lines rising from it. My ____6____ was terrible, but she laughed gently and pointed towards a pot behind the counter. Then she drew two bowls of different sizes. I chose the ____7____ one because I was not very hungry.

She wrote a number beside it. This was the ____8____, which I could understand. I ____9____ to show agreement, and she went to the kitchen.

The soup was warm and delicious. As I ate, I felt myself ____10____. A difficult moment had become a small conversation, even though neither of us had suddenly learned the other's language.

Before leaving, I asked her to say the name of the dish slowly. I repeated it until I could say it reasonably well. She wrote it beside my bowl, and I folded the paper into my pocket so I would ____11____ it.

Back with my host family, I showed them the picture. They enjoyed my account of the ____12____ as much as the drawing. The next afternoon, I returned and ordered using my new word. The waiter recognised me and drew a smiling face on the bill.

I still wanted to learn more vocabulary. But I stopped expecting my speech to be ____13____ before trying a simple exchange. A little patience and the ____14____ to ask could open a door. The paper bowl stayed in my travel notebook, reminding me how much a conversation can achieve once we ____15____.
questions.explanation: The host family hears about the attempt to communicate. No recipe, weather report or building description is given.
